WHEREAS, a geo-coding error resulted in $173,681,000 in CDBG-DR funds that should have been part of the City’s federal award being included in the County’s federal award instead (“Misallocated Funds”); and

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of St. Petersburg, Florida, that (I) the Community Development Block Grant -Disaster Recovery Agreement between the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), Pinellas County, Florida (“County”) and the City of St. Petersburg, Florida (“ City”) related to a geo-coding error that resulted in $173,681,000 in CDBG-DR funds that should have been part of the City’s federal award being included in the County’s federal award (“Misallocated Funds”) and (ii) the CDBG -DR Funds Coordination Agreement between the County and the City that establishes a coordinated and efficient framework for the use and oversight of the misallocated funds are hereby approved.

EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. The NPCSS Program (also referred to as ‘the Program’) is built to strengthen the community by helping nonprofits offer the care and support people need after disaster, so residents can recover and prepare for the future. This RFA, the first in a series of funding opportunities under the NPCSS Program, is specifically focused on identifying subrecipients who will provide mental health and wraparound support services as described in this document. This is not a grantmaking opportunity where organizations apply to meet their individual needs; this is a solicitation where the City is procuring a specific set of services to meet the needs of city residents. Non-Profit Community Support Services Program (CDBG-DR) Request for Applications: Mental Health 6 | Page 3.0 PROGRAM OVERVIEW 3.1 FUNDING AVAILABLE The maximum funding available for this RFA is $1,250,000. This is the funding available for all three core services combined, meaning each selected organization will receive an award below this maximum amount. Outlined below are the award caps for each Core Service type: • Case Management award: up to $725,000 • Assertive Outreach award: up to $175,000 • Clinical Mental Health Services award: up to $350,000 Each organization must submit a budget that does not exceed the maximum award cap for the Core Service type(s) for which they are applying. If an organization is applying to administer multiple Core Services, the submitted budget must not exceed the combined total of both Core Service award caps. For example, if an organization applies for Case Management and Assertive Outreach, the budget cannot exceed $900,000. In this scenario, the organization must still break out the budget into sections outlining which costs are related to Case Management and which costs are related to Assertive Outreach. items.title: 06 | EXISTING CONDITIONS + ANALYSIS TRAILS CROSSING MASTER PLAN 183182 CASE STUDY ANALYSIS 06 | EXISTING CONDITIONS + ANALYSIS Event + Festival Large-Scale Improved The Canopy is a 14.5-acre urban park taking shape beneath Interstate 4 in downtown Orlando, transforming a former surface parking area bounded by Church and Washington Streets and Hughey and Garland Avenues into a connected community hub. Formerly known as the Under-I Project, the park takes its name from Orlando’s tree canopy, with the stated goal of creating a vibrant, inclusive, and sustainable urban oasis beneath the interstate. The design, led by AECOM in partnership with the City of Orlando’s Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), evolved through public workshops and an online survey and is organized around six guiding principles — Connection, Safety, Community, Greenery, Mobility, and Artistic Immersion. These principles are translated into ﬁ ve landscaped zones anchored by seven large-scale metal tree sculptures, a digital projection and mapping system for nighttime video art, an integrated sound system, permanent restrooms, and a dedicated bike path. items.title: The goal is not simply to decorate City Hall, but to acquire a memorable work of public art that adds character to the plaza and reflects the creativity, diversity, and spirit of Gainesville. Site and Historical Context Gainesville City Hall has an important place in the city's civic and architectural history. An earlier city hall, dating to approximately 1928, served the community before the construction of the current complex. In 1968–1969, the City constructed a new City Hall and library complex in the Brutalist architectural style, characterized by textured concrete, geometric forms, and an expansive reflecting pool and water features. City Hall Plaza underwent a major revitalization through the Wild Spaces & Public Places half-cent sales tax program. The $1.8 million project replaced the aging 1960s water features and created a more accessible and inviting civic gathering space. The renovated plaza reopened in May 2026 and includes terraced seating, the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Hall of Fame Garden, and the Sister Cities Monument Garden. The artwork will occupy a prominent location on the front left wall of City Hall and will be visible from the public plaza. The approximate

Stormwater Utility System The stormwater system serves nearly 7,700 parcels. Due to minimal projected customer growth, baseline revenues are expected to stay flat at around $1.4 million annually through the forecast period. The FY 2026 budget relies on existing cash reserves to balance. While effective short-term, a long- term rate adjustment is required to avoid completely depleting these funds. Operating expenses have risen nearly 8% per year since 2021. The 2026 budget sits at $1.3 million and is projected to scale 3.8% annually to $1.6 million by 2031, driven by inflation, labor (4%), and health insurance (10%). The total stormwater capital improvement plan is $140.9 million (2026– 2031). $132.8 million will be covered externally via the Resiliency Fund. $8.1 million must be absorbed by the stormwater fund itself ($3.4 million via user rates and $4.8 million via new debt). The system is paying $256,000 annually on a 2015 revenue note, which will be paid off in 2030. To help fund the capital plan, a new State Revolving Fund (SRF) loan of roughly $353,000 annually will come online in 2030, seamlessly replacing the old debt.

Revenues and Trends - Ms. Schmidt reviewed the City’s revenue trends, noting total FY 2027 sources of approximately $85.4 million, including $32.8 million in the General Fund. She highlighted major revenue sources such as property taxes, EMS reimbursements, parking, utility and franchise revenues, sales tax, enterprise fund rates, and outstanding FEMA reimbursements. She also discussed the potential impact of Amendment 3 on homestead tax revenue and emphasized the City’s effort to right-size enterprise fund fees so services are funded by users rather than property tax subsidies.

Reclaimed Water System Mr. Ocasio reviewed key findings from the study. The system serves approximately 2,900 accounts. Rate revenue is projected to stay flat at around $1.1 million annually through FY 2030 due to minimal customer growth. Under existing rates, current revenues only cover standard operations and a portion of a $61,000 annual General Fund loan (payoff in 2039). Revenues are completely insufficient to fund capital investments. Rising Costs: Operating expenses have grown roughly 16% per year since 2021 and are projected to rise at 4.5% annually through FY 2030, driven by labor (4%), health insurance (10%), and county wholesale water rate increases (5%). The system requires $4.5 million between 2026 and 2031 for two major projects (lateral service pipe replacement and port installation), averaging $676,000 annually. The city bills based on parcel square footage rather than usage, making direct comparisons to other cities difficult. However, under the proposed changes, the rate would align closely with regional averages for heavy irrigation (25,000 gallons).

SUMMARY: On March 10, 2026, the Village adopted an ordinance annexing approximately 446.14 acres of land, known as Artistry Lakes. The County objected to the annexation because the annexation area does not meet the requirements of Section 171.043, Florida Statutes. On March 26, 2026, the County passed a resolution initiating the Conflict Resolution Procedures under Chapter 164. Florida Statutes. On February 10, 2026, after discussions with the County, the Village initiated the Interlocal Service Boundary Agreement (ISBA) process to negotiate the terms under which the subject property and adjacent properties will be annexed. The County adopted its responding resolution on February 26, 2026. While the Village approved the ISBA, the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) denied it on August 26, 2026. On September 30th, 2026 the County Administrator and the Village Manager met per Ch. 164 Conflict Resolution Proceedings. Both the County Administrator and the Village Manager agreed to bring the ILA to their respective governing bodies. The County also agreed to bring the PBA to the BCC at the same time as the ILA. The Village Council approved the ILA on October 13, 2026.

Staff recommends motion to approve: an allocation of $2,000,000 of State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funding for the Flood Disaster Assistance Program (FDAP) to provide financial assistance to eligible homeowners who suffered flood-related damages to homestead properties. Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. Per SHIP requirements, eligibility will be limited to homeowners with incomes no greater than 140% of Area Median Income (AMI) (currently $179,900 for an eligible household of four [4] persons).

Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. Although the Engineer’s Opinion of Probable Construction Cost (OPCC) was $1,544,000.00 (Completed April 2025), material and equipment price volatility, inflation, limitation on pool of qualified contractors, and construction market condition costs have increased. Hazen and Sawyer analyzed the bids in detail and determined them to be reasonable within current market conditions, see attached Engineer’s Bid Price Review. Specifically, Hazen and Sawyer noted that the major price difference between the OPCC and the bid was related to the steel canopies and skimmer systems. Hazen and Sawyer stated that there is ongoing variability in the metals market, and limited competition with a constrained vendor pool. City staff recommend awarding Bid No. 25-65- 06-CM to RF Environmental. Approval of this award will replace critical components of the DAF thickening system, restore reliable solids processing capacity, and ensure continued compliance with wastewater treatment requirements at the Sawgrass WWTP.

Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. Per SHIP requirements, eligibility will be limited to homeowners with incomes no greater than 140% of Area Median Income (AMI) (currently $179,900 for an eligible household of four [4] persons).
